paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning involves learning how an environment behaves and choosing actions using that learned model. These two activities depend on each other: a policy determines which experiences are collected, while the model influences which policy looks promising. This paper organizes that interaction as a game to make algorithm design easier to reason about.

The game has two players. The policy player seeks high rewards according to the current model, and the model player tries to explain real observations collected by the policy. The authors show that finding an approximate equilibrium of this game can yield a near-optimal policy for the actual environment. They develop two algorithm families using ideas from Stackelberg games.

Experiments suggest that these algorithms achieve leading sample efficiency while matching the eventual performance of model-free policy gradient methods. They also handle high-dimensional tasks such as dexterous hand manipulation. The contribution connects a theoretical solution concept with practical ways to coordinate model fitting and policy improvement.
icml-2020-a-game-theoretic-framework-for.tldr: A game between policy learning and model fitting yields algorithms with theoretical support and promising empirical sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in a graph can require labels that are expensive to collect. Active learning addresses this by choosing which nodes a person should label next. The paper targets graphs with node attributes, where existing graph neural network approaches can struggle without a substantial labeled validation set for selecting their settings.

The proposed method predicts labels with graph cognizant logistic regression, which is equivalent to a linearized graph convolutional network. It chooses queries by maximizing the expected reduction in prediction error. To shorten the wait between labeling requests, it computes the next query while the person is still labeling the current one.

For situations starting with almost no labels, the authors also combine label propagation and linearized graph network predictions through adaptive model averaging. Experiments on five public benchmarks show significant improvements over the compared leading approaches, and an application to a private microwave link network illustrates practical use. Together, the components address both label efficiency and the pace of human interaction.
icml-2020-active-learning-on-attributed-.tldr: A graph-based active learner combines targeted label requests, adaptive predictions, and advance query computation to improve classification with limited labels.

paragraphs: Automated machine learning often searches among structures built from sophisticated components designed by experts. AutoML-Zero asks whether the search can reach deeper, discovering complete learning algorithms from basic mathematical operations. Its broad search space reduces the amount of machine learning structure that people must specify in advance.

The framework uses evolutionary search to explore that space. Despite the large number of possible programs, it can discover two-layer neural networks trained through backpropagation. Evolving algorithms directly on target tasks, including variants of CIFAR-10, produces algorithms that outperform those simple networks. Successful candidates contain techniques such as bilinear interactions, gradient normalization, and weight averaging.

The evolved algorithms also respond to task conditions: dropout-like behavior appears when training data is scarce. These results suggest that the search can recover useful learning mechanisms as well as network structures. The authors present the findings as preliminary successes, supporting the possibility of broader algorithm discovery without claiming that basic-operation search has solved automated machine learning in general.
icml-2020-automl-zero-evolving-machine-l.tldr: AutoML-Zero uses evolutionary search over basic mathematical operations to discover learning algorithms and task-adapted training techniques.

paragraphs: Many decisions affect both an organization's interests and the welfare of others. Evaluating a policy with only one objective can obscure that tension. This paper studies policies that explicitly balance a private objective, such as profit, against a public objective, such as social welfare, when the available predictions are imperfect.

The authors analyze a class of policies built from learned scores. These policies trace an empirical Pareto frontier: a collection of estimated trade-offs between the two objectives. Their theory identifies optimal strategies within this class and bounds how score inaccuracies distort the frontier. This makes the quality of the underlying predictions part of the analysis of decision quality.

The paper also establishes an equivalence between optimal strategies and a broad class of profit-maximizing policies subject to fairness constraints. Empirical studies in online content recommendation and sustainable abalone fisheries illustrate the approach in different settings. The results clarify how competing objectives and noisy data jointly shape welfare-aware decisions.
icml-2020-balancing-competing-objectives.tldr: The paper characterizes score-based profit–welfare trade-offs and bounds how prediction errors affect those decisions.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is often implemented without replacement, so examples are not repeatedly sampled within the same pass. Much of its theory instead analyzes sampling with replacement. This paper sharpens the convergence guarantees for the practical sampling scheme, focusing on strongly convex objectives formed by summing n smooth functions over T iterations.

Earlier results left a gap between the fastest proven convergence and the limits suggested by lower bounds. When the summed objective is quadratic, the authors establish an upper bound of order 1/T² + n²/T³. This matches the stated lower bound and improves the previous quadratic result, whose second term involved n³ rather than n².

For the broader class of strongly convex sums of smooth functions, the paper proves a lower bound of order n/T², matching the existing upper rate. The two results distinguish the quadratic setting from the general smooth setting. They explain which convergence improvements are achievable within these classes and where the known guarantees already reach the theoretical limit.
icml-2020-closing-the-convergence-gap-of.tldr: Matching upper and lower bounds resolve convergence-rate gaps for SGD without replacement in quadratic and general strongly convex settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning across a communicating network of agents, each receiving independent data from the same unknown distribution. It combines distributed gradient descent with random features and implicit regularization. Random features reduce memory requirements and give every agent a shared parameterization, addressing implementation difficulties in decentralized kernel regression.

Under source and capacity assumptions, the authors bound each agent's predictive performance with high probability. The bounds account for the step size, training iterations, number of random features, and the communication matrix's inverse spectral gap. Tuning these quantities yields statistical rates that are minimax optimal relative to the total amount of data across the network.

The algorithm offers a linear improvement in memory cost over single-machine gradient descent. A linear computational speedup is also available for any network topology when each agent holds enough data relative to network size and inverse spectral gap. Simulations examine how features, iterations, and sample counts affect prediction, connecting the theoretical choices to observed behavior.
icml-2020-decentralised-learning-with-ra.tldr: Random features support decentralized learning with optimal statistical rates and conditional linear computational speedups.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy trained for one set of environment dynamics may need substantial new interaction when those dynamics change. This paper proposes Policy-Dynamics Value Functions, or PD-VF, to support faster adaptation. The central idea is to estimate how well different policies will perform in different environments within a shared learned representation.

During training, an ensemble of conventional reinforcement learning policies gathers experience across training environments. That experience is used to learn embeddings of both policies and environments. A value function then predicts cumulative reward conditioned on both embeddings, allowing the system to evaluate policy–environment combinations through the learned model.

At test time, a few actions provide enough information to infer an embedding for the new environment. The method then selects a policy by maximizing the learned value function, without further environment interaction for that selection step. Results on a set of MuJoCo domains demonstrate rapid adaptation to previously unseen dynamics, showing how learned performance predictions can reduce the interaction needed for adaptation.
icml-2020-fast-adaptation-to-new-environ.tldr: PD-VF learns policy–environment reward predictions to select policies after only a few actions in a new environment.

paragraphs: Tasks such as data summarization and influence maximization can be expressed as choosing a valuable collection under constraints. Monotone submodular objectives capture a form of diminishing returns while ensuring that adding elements does not reduce value. This paper studies how to optimize such objectives under matroid constraints while preserving differential privacy for sensitive individual data.

For monotone submodular maximization, the authors provide an algorithm with a 1 − 1/e approximation guarantee, improving the approximation guarantee of previous private results. The algorithm uses an almost cubic number of function evaluations. The result addresses solution quality and evaluation cost together within a privacy-preserving optimization framework.

The paper also treats monotone k-submodular functions, a generalization of submodularity. It introduces the first differentially private algorithm with a one-half approximation guarantee under matroid constraints. That ratio is asymptotically tight, and the method needs an almost linear number of function evaluations. These contributions establish distinct quality and computational guarantees for the two related optimization settings.
icml-2020-fast-and-private-submodular-an.tldr: The paper gives differentially private approximation algorithms for constrained submodular and k-submodular maximization with improved or tight guarantees.

paragraphs: Training data can contain both social bias and deliberately poisoned examples. The paper argues that existing fairness methods may treat poisoning as another bias to correct, causing substantial performance degradation. FR-Train addresses fairness and resistance to poisoning together, so efforts to mitigate bias also account for the reliability of the training data.

The authors first interpret an existing adversarial fairness-training method through mutual information. They use that interpretation to design an additional discriminator that identifies poisoned data with help from a clean validation set. Reducing the influence of these examples allows the training process to pursue fairness while defending against corrupted supervision.

In the reported experiments, FR-Train experiences almost no loss of fairness or accuracy under data poisoning. The clean validation set is an explicit part of the approach, and the authors demonstrate how crowdsourcing can construct such sets. They also release benchmark datasets. The findings support treating fairness and robustness as interacting training objectives rather than addressing data bias without considering poisoning.
icml-2020-fr-train-a-mutual-information-.tldr: FR-Train uses a clean validation set and an additional discriminator to jointly mitigate bias and reduce poisoned data's influence.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a reinforcement learning agent needs another signal to guide exploration. This paper builds that signal from uncertainty about environment dynamics. Its approach uses an implicit generative model to represent a range of plausible explanations of how the environment changes in response to the agent's actions.

Each draw from the generator produces an entire neural network representing a dynamics function. Multiple draws approximate a Bayesian posterior over dynamics models. The agent compares their predictions and uses prediction variance as an intrinsic reward for exploration. The generator is trained through an algorithm based on amortized Stein Variational Gradient Descent.

The authors evaluate the method on pure exploration tasks and a downstream task, comparing it with leading intrinsic-reward approaches, including two methods using ensembles of dynamics models. On challenging exploration tasks, the proposed method consistently improves exploration data efficiency over the compared approaches. The results support using generated dynamics hypotheses to turn uncertainty into a useful guide for collecting experience.
icml-2020-implicit-generative-modeling-f.tldr: A generator of neural dynamics models supplies uncertainty-based exploration rewards that improve data efficiency in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Neural image reconstruction systems solve inverse problems by turning measurements into images, but adversarial disturbances can undermine their output. This paper modifies training to improve robustness. An auxiliary network generates adversarial examples, while the reconstruction network learns through a min-max objective to withstand the resulting challenges.

The authors argue that attacks on inverse problem solvers should be studied in measurement space, where reconstruction inputs reside, rather than in signal space. For a linear reconstruction scheme, they show that the min-max formulation produces a regularized solution based on filtering singular values. This solution suppresses adversarial effects, and numerical experiments confirm convergence to it.

The empirical study extends to nonlinear compressive sensing with a deep network on two standard datasets and to a published low-dose x-ray CT reconstruction algorithm using anonymized clinical data. The proposed training approach significantly improves robustness over other deep reconstruction methods in these experiments. The work connects an analyzable linear solution with evidence from more complex reconstruction systems.
icml-2020-improving-robustness-of-deep-l.tldr: Adversarial min-max training improves image reconstruction robustness, supported by a linear analysis and nonlinear reconstruction experiments.

paragraphs: An explanation can reveal that a neural network gives importance to the wrong features, yet that insight alone does not change the model. This paper focuses on the next step: giving practitioners a way to act on what an explanation reveals. Its objective is to improve predictions by incorporating relevant domain knowledge during learning.

The proposed method, contextual decomposition explanation penalization, or CDEP, uses explanations as a channel for that knowledge. When a practitioner identifies an incorrect assignment of feature importance, explanation penalties provide a means to correct it. The approach connects the diagnosis of a model's behavior to a training intervention aimed at changing that behavior.

The authors demonstrate improved performance across toy and real datasets. These findings show that explanations can have a practical role in model development beyond helping people inspect predictions. The contribution is a method for translating knowledge about inappropriate feature importance into learning guidance, with empirical evidence that doing so can improve predictive accuracy in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-interpretations-are-useful-pen.tldr: CDEP turns explanation-based judgments about incorrect feature importance into training penalties that can improve predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: An agent may not know which outcomes a user values or which states are unsafe, while asking the user for guidance is costly. ReQueST learns a reward model by asking about hypothetical behavior. It begins with a generative model of initial states and a forward dynamics model trained on off-policy data.

These models synthesize trajectories that the user labels with rewards, and a neural network learns to predict those rewards. The method actively constructs questions by optimizing tractable proxies for their information value. Because the candidate behaviors are generated through models, producing these queries requires no interaction with the environment.

Evaluations use simulated users in a state-based navigation task and the image-based Car Racing game. ReQueST significantly outperforms prior methods at learning rewards that transfer to environments with different initial-state distributions. The experiments also show safe training of unsafe-state detection and correction of reward hacking before deployment. The findings support using carefully chosen hypothetical behavior to acquire useful feedback without executing those behaviors.
icml-2020-learning-human-objectives-by-e.tldr: ReQueST synthesizes informative hypothetical behaviors for user feedback, learning transferable reward models without executing the queried behaviors.

paragraphs: Training large convolutional networks can take long enough to restrict experimentation. Lower-precision arithmetic can reduce that cost, but the paper identifies vanishing gradients as a reason accuracy may suffer. MuPPET addresses the tension by changing numerical precision during training rather than committing the whole process to one low-precision representation.

The strategy uses multiple numerical regimes, including low-precision fixed-point representations. A runtime mechanism decides when to move between them, forming a multilevel optimization approach. This extends the two-level mixed-precision pattern described in the abstract and adapts the training process to the computational capabilities of the target hardware.

On ImageNet training for AlexNet, ResNet18, and GoogLeNet targeting an NVIDIA Turing GPU, MuPPET matches standard full-precision accuracy. It achieves training speedups of up to 1.84 times and an average of 1.58 times across those networks. The paper also reports improved energy efficiency. These results show that adaptive precision choices can preserve final accuracy while reducing training cost in the tested configuration.
icml-2020-multi-precision-policy-enforce.tldr: MuPPET switches numerical precision during training, matching full-precision accuracy with an average 1.58× speedup across three tested networks.

paragraphs: A graph generator should reproduce meaningful patterns in an input network without needing every pattern specified by hand. NetGAN approaches this by training a generative adversarial network to learn the input graph's random-walk distribution. This paper investigates which part of that system actually accounts for its ability to generalize.

The authors identify a low-rank approximation of the logits of the random-walk transition matrix as the source of the relevant inductive bias. They progressively simplify NetGAN, removing components including the adversarial network itself. The resulting formulation makes the structural assumption behind the method more explicit and easier to understand.

The simplified approach achieves comparable generalization results while running orders of magnitude faster and being easier to adapt. The finding changes the explanation of NetGAN's success: the essential mechanism identified by this study is a matrix approximation embedded in the procedure. Making that mechanism visible provides both a computational simplification and a clearer account of how the graph model generalizes.
icml-2020-netgan-without-gan-from-random.tldr: A low-rank matrix reformulation preserves NetGAN-like generalization while removing the GAN and greatly reducing computation.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows offer a way to build expressive probability distributions in high dimensions. Much of their development has focused on Euclidean spaces, but some quantities naturally belong to spaces with different geometry. The paper highlights angles as a motivating example and studies flows on tori and spheres.

The authors propose and compare flow constructions designed for those spaces, describing them as expressive and numerically stable. Their construction is recursive in dimension: flows in higher-dimensional spaces are built from lower-dimensional components. The starting components include flows on circles, closed intervals, or spheres, giving the approach a common organizing principle across the geometries considered.

The contribution expands the settings in which flow-based distribution modeling can be formulated around the geometry of the variables themselves. Its emphasis is on constructing suitable distributions and comparing the resulting flows. By connecting higher-dimensional models to simpler geometric building blocks, the paper provides a structured route to expressive probability models beyond the Euclidean setting that dominates the prior literature.
icml-2020-normalizing-flows-on-tori-and-.tldr: The paper constructs expressive, numerically stable normalizing flows on tori and spheres through recursion over dimension.

paragraphs: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees, or BART, provide a flexible approach to prediction. This paper examines a different question: whether BART also supports statistically valid uncertainty statements. Accurate estimation of a regression function and reliable inference about quantities derived from that function are related goals, but establishing one does not by itself establish the other.

The analysis considers nonparametric regression with fixed covariates and focuses on smooth linear functionals of the regression surface. These are particular summaries of the underlying function. The authors establish semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises results, studying the asymptotic normality that makes inference about those summaries possible.

The findings show that BART can support valid statistical inference beyond achieving optimal estimation rates in the setting studied. Their importance lies in supplying theoretical justification for uncertainty quantification, an area the abstract identifies as less developed than approximation and estimation theory. The result concerns asymptotic behavior for the specified functionals and regression framework, giving a precise scope to the inference claim.
icml-2020-on-semi-parametric-inference-f.tldr: The paper establishes asymptotic inference guarantees for smooth linear summaries of BART regression functions with fixed covariates.

paragraphs: Multi-output learning predicts a vector rather than a single scalar. This framework includes predicting several numerical targets, selecting among multiple classes, and assigning multiple labels. The paper develops generalization theory for these problems, aiming to describe how accurately learned predictors can perform beyond their supervised training data.

The central tool is a self-bounding Lipschitz condition on the loss function. It connects the classical Lipschitz condition to a multidimensional smoothness condition through a continuous range of possibilities. Under this condition, the authors derive optimistic learning bounds that achieve minimax-optimal rates up to logarithmic factors. The guarantee is therefore tied to a specified property of the loss.

The proof combines local Rademacher complexity with a minoration inequality. As a concrete application, the authors obtain a state-of-the-art generalization bound for multiclass gradient boosting. The contribution supplies a shared analytical condition for several multi-output settings and shows that it can produce strong guarantees for an established learning method.
icml-2020-optimistic-bounds-for-multi-ou.tldr: A self-bounding loss condition yields nearly minimax-optimal generalization bounds for multi-output learning and a strong multiclass boosting guarantee.

paragraphs: Long training and large networks often work well in ordinary deep learning, even when overfitting might seem likely. This paper empirically examines whether that experience carries over to adversarial training, where models learn to resist worst-case input perturbations. It finds that overfitting can substantially damage performance against attacks on unseen data.

The effect appears across SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, with both L-infinity and L-2 perturbations. Based on these observations, the authors show that early stopping can match the performance gains of virtually all recent adversarial-training improvements considered in their study. This makes the point at which training ends an important part of evaluating robustness methods.

The authors also observe double descent in adversarially trained models, but find that it does not explain the overfitting they identify. They examine regularization, data augmentation, and other remedies; no approach used alone significantly improves on early stopping's gains. The empirical findings emphasize training duration as a consequential factor in robust generalization.
icml-2020-overfitting-in-adversarially-r.tldr: Adversarial training can severely overfit, and early stopping matches many reported algorithmic gains in the paper's empirical study.

paragraphs: This paper studies an attacker who changes a reinforcement learning environment during training to induce a chosen policy. The victim seeks to maximize average reward over an undiscounted, infinite horizon. The attacker can alter rewards or transition dynamics and aims to make those changes stealthy according to specified attack-cost measures.

The authors formulate the search for an optimal stealthy attack as an optimization problem. They give sufficient technical conditions for an attack to be feasible and establish lower and upper bounds on its cost. These results connect whether a target policy can be induced with how much the environment must be manipulated.

The framework covers both offline planning in a poisoned environment and online learning with poisoned feedback under regret minimization. The results show that, under mild conditions, an attacker can successfully teach any target policy. The security concern is that an agent pursuing its stated learning objective can still acquire attacker-selected behavior when the training environment itself has been changed.
icml-2020-policy-teaching-via-environmen.tldr: An optimization framework shows how training-environment poisoning can induce attacker-chosen policies under sufficient feasibility conditions.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines a small supply of labels for the actual prediction target with a larger supply of weaker labels. This paper studies how those additional labels affect generalization on the target task. Its focus is a two-stage procedure: first pretrain using weak labels, then fine-tune using the strong labels.

The authors show that this procedure can yield a learning rate of order 1/n, where n counts strongly labeled examples. That acceleration can occur even when strong labels alone support only a rate of order 1/√n. Here, the improvement concerns how learning performance scales with labeled data, rather than a claim about computational training speed.

The benefit depends continuously on both the number of weak labels and the relationship between the weak and strong tasks. It is therefore a conditional acceleration, not an automatic consequence of adding any auxiliary labels. Experiments across several tasks reflect the theoretical results, illustrating how suitable weak supervision can make scarce target labels more effective.
icml-2020-strength-from-weakness-fast-le.tldr: Weak-label pretraining can improve target-task learning rates from O(1/√n) to O(1/n), depending on label availability and task relationships.

paragraphs: Selecting the best k items from noisy comparisons requires deciding which pairs to compare and when enough evidence has been collected. This paper studies an active learner that can compare any pair, receives independent noisy outcomes, and chooses subsequent comparisons using previous results. The goal is reliable selection with as few comparisons as possible.

The analysis covers approximate and exact selection under strong stochastic transitivity and a stochastic triangle inequality. For probably approximately correct selection, the authors establish a lower bound on required comparisons and provide an algorithm matching it up to a constant factor. This identifies the achievable sample complexity within the stated assumptions.

For exact selection, they prove a worst-instance lower bound and construct two algorithms using their approximate-selection methods. The single-best-item algorithm is optimal up to a loglog factor, while the algorithm for arbitrary k is optimal up to a log factor. These results separate the costs of approximate and exact answers while giving near-optimal procedures for both.
icml-2020-the-sample-complexity-of-best-.tldr: The paper gives optimal or nearly optimal comparison bounds for approximate and exact top-k selection under specified stochastic ordering assumptions.

paragraphs: Choosing a classifier can involve a tension between predictive performance and understanding its decisions. Model-Agnostic Linear Competitors, or MALC, combines an existing black-box classifier with competing linear models for multiclass prediction. The aim is to bring interpretable components into the decision process while retaining access to the black-box model's predictive capabilities.

The authors formulate MALC training as a convex optimization problem. Its objective balances prediction accuracy with transparency, defined specifically as the percentage of data captured by the linear models. This definition makes transparency an explicit quantity in training and gives users a way to adjust the balance between the two goals.

Experiments show that MALC offers more flexibility in this balance than choosing a purely interpretable or purely black-box model. A human evaluation also finds that more users are likely to choose MALC because of that flexibility. The result supports a hybrid approach in which the extent of interpretable decision-making is itself part of model design.
icml-2020-transparency-promotion-with-mo.tldr: MALC combines linear classifiers with a black-box model to explicitly balance predictive accuracy and interpretable coverage.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve resistance to perturbed inputs while worsening accuracy on ordinary inputs. One explanation assumes that the model class contains no predictor capable of doing both well. This paper investigates a different possibility through linear regression, where the optimal linear predictor has zero error on both ordinary and perturbed inputs.

The authors characterize how augmentation changes standard error in this setting. They show that the error can increase even when the added perturbations receive noiseless observations from the optimal predictor. Thus, a trade-off can arise despite the existence of a predictor that satisfies both objectives and despite correct supervision on the augmented examples.

The paper then proves that robust self-training improves robust error without sacrificing standard error for noiseless linear regression. Neural network experiments on CIFAR-10 also find improvements in both errors across random and adversarial rotations and adversarial L-infinity perturbations. The theoretical and empirical results identify a way to mitigate the trade-off, with the formal guarantee confined to the stated regression setting.
icml-2020-understanding-and-mitigating-t.tldr: Augmentation can harm ordinary accuracy even when a perfect robust predictor exists, while robust self-training can mitigate this trade-off.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation of the output; invariant networks keep the output unchanged. Such structures are useful across sequences, images, sets, and graphs. This paper asks how expressive these constrained networks can be, focusing on multilayer perceptrons with a single hidden layer.

The main theorem establishes universality for a broad class of these networks. In particular, a regular group action on the hidden layer is sufficient for universal equivariance or invariance. This provides a structural condition under which respecting a symmetry still permits universal approximation of the corresponding symmetry-respecting functions.

Several consequences follow. Some steerable convolutional networks become universal, and equivariant multilayer perceptrons have unconditional universality for Abelian groups. The authors also establish universality using high-order hidden layers, giving both general and group-specific bounds on the required order. These are expressiveness guarantees: they clarify which architectural structures suffice to represent the desired class of functions.
icml-2020-universal-equivariant-multilay.tldr: The paper proves sufficient structural conditions for single-hidden-layer equivariant networks to achieve universal approximation.
